title: A Blank Is Not a No: A Two-Person Plant Check That Records What You Actually Saw
subtitle: Choose one plant feature, compare separate observations, and learn why an honest field note records uncertainty as carefully as presence.
imageAlt: Two friends pause beside a flowering shrub, each writing a separate observation in a small notebook.
imageConcept: A natural, close-up scene of two friends standing beside an easily accessible garden shrub or park plant. Each has a small notebook and looks carefully at the same branch without pointing or conferring; the emphasis is on the shared pause and independent notes, not a dramatic landscape or a staged scientific setup.
body: The useful difference between “no” and “not checked

Choose one plant you can observe safely and one feature you can define plainly: Are any flowers open? Are leaves unfolding? Are fruits visible? Then make a small note that distinguishes what you found from what you didn’t examine. In a field record, “no” means you looked for the feature and did not see it. “Not checked” means you did not look. “Uncertain” means you looked but cannot tell. A blank is useful, too: it can mark a question you have not answered, rather than quietly becoming an answer of its own.

That distinction is the heart of this two-person exercise. It is not a test of who notices more, or an attempt to diagnose the season from one walk. It is a way to practice describing evidence accurately—and to discover how two attentive people can look at the same plant and leave with different, equally honest notes. The USA National Phenology Network (USA-NPN) uses these response distinctions in its observer guidance, alongside recording the date of each observation [1].
Start with a plant you can observe comfortably

Pick one individual plant that both people can reach visually without stepping off a path, climbing, touching unfamiliar growth, or entering private or restricted land. A familiar shrub in a yard, a tree beside a public walkway, or a plant in a community garden with permission can all work. If either person has limited mobility or prefers not to go outdoors, choose a plant visible from a window or a seated position. The point is attentive looking, not covering distance.

Agree on the plant before you begin. If there are several similar shrubs nearby, identify the one you mean by a non-sensitive description: “the shrub beside the bench” or “the potted plant by the entrance.” Avoid picking, bending, or moving parts to make the feature easier to see. Decide on one feature that can be described in a sentence. “Are any flowers open?” is easier to answer consistently than “Does it look like spring?” Specific questions reduce guesswork and make it easier to compare notes without turning impressions into claims.

Each person should look and record an answer before discussing what they see. Give it a minute or two, or agree on another comfortable amount of time. Keep the task narrow: look for open flowers, for example, rather than scanning every leaf, bud, and insect on the plant. A phone photo can help you remember what you examined, but it is optional; a written note is enough for this exercise.

Use four response options: **yes**, **no**, **uncertain**, or **not checked**. If you can see one or more open flowers, write yes. If you examined the plant for open flowers and saw none, write no. If distance, glare, overlapping branches, or your own uncertainty prevents a clear answer, write uncertain. If you ran out of time or never looked at the relevant part, write not checked. Do not use “no” to mean “I don’t know.” USA-NPN’s documentation explains these distinctions for observations in its Nature’s Notebook program [1].

Keep the record small: plant description, feature, date, answer, and any useful condition such as “viewed from the path.” That is enough to make the note intelligible later.
Compare notes without turning them into a verdict

Now share what you wrote. If both answers match, you have a useful point of agreement about that particular observation. If one person wrote yes and the other uncertain, resist the urge to settle the matter by persuasion. Look again together if it is safe and comfortable, or keep both original answers and add a note that you rechecked. If you agree that the feature was visible on a second look, record that as a new observation—not as proof that the first person should have seen it.

Disagreement can point to a practical issue: one observer may have been looking from farther away, a branch may have blocked the view, or “open flower” may not have meant quite the same thing to both people. Make the feature definition more precise next time. The exercise works best when neither person is assigned the role of expert and the other the role of learner. Different eyesight, vantage points, and experience are part of what the comparison can reveal.
What a single walk can—and cannot—tell you

A careful note documents one observation at a particular time. It does not establish when a plant first flowered, how long flowering lasts, or whether the season is changing. Those questions depend on observations made over time, with dates and methods clear enough to compare. In a forest-phenology study, researchers retained “yes” records only when they were preceded by a “no” within an acceptable time period, illustrating how paired observations can help locate a phenophase transition [3]. That is a study-specific example, not a rule that every informal observer needs to follow.

For research and resource management, consistency matters. A 2014 paper on standardized phenology monitoring describes protocols designed to make plant and animal observations more comparable across locations and studies [2]. A couple’s walk is not a standardized monitoring program, and one note should not be presented as scientific evidence of a trend. Its value is more modest and immediate: it leaves a truthful record of what each observer checked, on what date, and with what confidence.
If you want to contribute beyond your notebook

If this small exercise leaves you interested in making formal observations, join a project through its own current instructions rather than treating your note as if it already meets a project’s protocol. Start by checking the project’s species list, feature definitions, observation schedule, and directions for recording answers. For Nature’s Notebook, use the current USA-NPN guidance and account setup; other projects may ask for different details or use different methods [1]. Follow the protocol as written, especially when a question is not a simple yes or no.

There is also a question of whether a location should be shared at all. A personal note can stay private, and a useful observation does not have to be uploaded. Do not disclose sensitive locations or culturally significant seasonal knowledge without appropriate permission and guidance. Choosing not to publish is a valid part of responsible observation.
Leave the notebook with the real answer

Try the exercise once this week, or choose a plant you already pass regularly. Agree on one visible feature, look separately, and write the date beside each answer. When you compare, ask a practical question rather than “Who got it right?”: Did we look at the same part of the plant? Was the feature clear enough to define? Would a different viewing angle help? If you did not check, leave it as not checked. If you cannot tell, let uncertain stand. If you looked and found none, record no.

Keep the two notes, including any difference between them. You have not produced a verdict on the plant or a pattern across the season. You have made something smaller and more dependable: a record that says what was observed, what was not, and where doubt remains. That is a good place to begin looking again.
